flawed_step: Step 1: going from "every edge lies in exactly one triangle" (a local condition on edges) to "some vertex is adjacent to all other vertices" (a global condition). The friendship theorem needs every pair of vertices to have exactly one common neighbour. The edge condition is weaker and does not imply that. It does not even make the graph connected.
counterexample: Two disjoint triangles: each edge is in exactly one triangle, but no vertex is adjacent to all 6 vertices. A connected example is K3 □ K3, the 3×3 rook's graph. Two vertices are adjacent when they share a row or a column. An edge within a row has exactly one common neighbour, the third vertex of that row, so the edge lies only in the row triangle; the same holds for columns. Every vertex has degree 4 out of 8 others, so no vertex is universal.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. It mixes up the edge condition with the hypothesis of the friendship theorem, which is that every pair of vertices has exactly one common neighbour. The proof fails at the first step, and there are clear counterexamples: two disjoint triangles, and the connected graph K3 □ K3.
